lesson.title: Relative Clauses in Depth
lesson.subtitle: que, quien (after prepositions: la persona con quien hablo), lo que, and donde

hook.title: Never End a Spanish Sentence with a Dangling Preposition!
hook.content: In casual English, we often strand prepositions at the very end of a sentence: 'the friend I am speaking **with**', 'the person the gift is **for**'. In Spanish, **a preposition can NEVER be stranded at the end of a clause**! Instead, the preposition stays right in front of **quien** ('whom'): el amigo **con quien** hablo ('the friend with whom I speak'), la persona **para quien** es el regalo ('the person for whom the gift is')!

pattern.title: Summary of All Four Relative Connectors
pattern.content:
1) **que** = who / whom / which / that (default for both people and things!).
2) **[preposition] + quien** = with whom / for whom / to whom (con quien, para quien, a quien).
3) **lo que** = what ('the thing that').
4) **donde** (no accent!) = where ('la ciudad donde vivo' = 'the city where I live')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: the friend with whom I speak (never strand con!)
the mother for whom the gift is
matching_pairs.german: la madre para quien es el regalo

matching_pairs.english: the city where I live (unaccented donde)

exercises.target_answer: el amigo con quien hablo, la madre para quien es el regalo, la ciudad donde vivo, lo que comprendo, el libro que tengo
exercises.meaning: the friend with whom I speak (never strand con!), the mother for whom the gift is, the city where I live (unaccented donde), what (the thing that) I understand, the book that I have
exercises.explanation: Prepositions always stand directly in front of quien — never at the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: How does Spanish express 'the friend I am speaking with'?
options: el amigo con quien hablo (or con el que hablo)
exercises.target_answer: el amigo con quien hablo (or con el que hablo)
exercises.meaning: the friend with whom I speak
exercises.explanation: Spanish never strands a preposition at the end of a clause; place con right before quien: con quien hablo!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'It is the city where I live'
exercises.meaning: It is the city where I live
exercises.explanation: Es la ciudad + donde (unstressed connector) + vivo.

exercises.idea: say: 'He is the friend with whom I speak'
cues: He is the friend → Es el amigo
idea_parts: He is the friend → Es el amigo
with whom I speak → con quien hablo
exercises.target_answer: Es el amigo con quien hablo
exercises.meaning: He is the friend with whom I speak
exercises.explanation: Es el amigo con quien hablo.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Es la persona con quien hablé ayer
exercises.target_answer: Es la persona con quien hablé ayer
exercises.meaning: He/she is the person with whom I spoke yesterday
cues: It is the person: Es la persona
exercises.explanation: Es la persona con quien hablé ayer.

summary.outcome: Build relative clauses with que, preposition + quien, lo que, and donde without stranding prepositions.

use_example.german: Es el amigo con quien hablé ayer en la ciudad donde vivo.
use_example.english: He is the friend with whom I spoke yesterday in the city where I live.

summary.takeaway: Keep prepositions right in front of quien (con quien, para quien) — never at the end of the sentence!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next branch ([5101] Hypothetical Situations): expand conditional -ía and subjunctive sentences!

qué.etymology_derivation: Latin quid → qué. Stressed in questions (accented qué), unstressed as conjunction (que).

quién.etymology_derivation: Has a plural form quiénes when asking about multiple people!

lo.etymology_derivation: Latin illum → lo. Walks one step to the left of conjugated verbs: I it want.

dónde.etymology_derivation: Latin dē + unde ('from where') → dónde. Carries written accent in questions.

con.english_meaning: with (conmigo: with me, contigo: with you)
con.etymology_derivation: Latin cum — the prefix in connect, combine, companion.

para.english_meaning: for (recipient, destination, deadline), in order to
para.etymology_derivation: Old Spanish pora (por + a) — think of para as a forward arrow pointing at the recipient, destination, deadline, or goal ('in order to').

hablar.english_meaning: to speak, to talk (hablo: I speak)
hablar.etymology_derivation: Latin fabulārī (to converse, tell stories — English fable and fabulous) shifted initial f- to silent h-: hablar!

vivir.etymology_derivation: Latin vīvere — English vivid, revive, survive.
